notes:
I've written notes for all 19 verses below, with a source link after each point.

**Gaps:**
- I didn't find anything usable from the Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox, netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org sites, or from any debated popular teaching (prosperity, word of faith and so on). Those sections are left out.
- The Methodist voice is Whedon's commentary on StudyLight. I didn't reach Wesley's own notes.
- The Whedon page and the full Precept Austin page came back without the markers I use for formal citations. Their points are in my own words with the link only, and are worth a quick check against the pages.
- I couldn't find Gill's comments on vv. 5–6. Where a tradition is named, it's my label for the commentator; the pages don't say it.

---

**v. 1**
- This story sits beside chapter 9 on purpose. In both, David is kind to the son of a recently dead royal father, one inside God's covenant (Mephibosheth) and one outside it (Hanun) (Bergen, quoted). Ammon descended from one of Lot's daughters. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-10-commentary
- Whedon (Methodist): Ammon bordered Moab, and Jephthah and Saul had both beaten it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/2-samuel-10.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik: David's kindness to Mephibosheth in the previous chapter didn't end his kind works. Here he showed kindness towards a pagan king because he sympathized with the loss of his father. He also acted on it rather than just feeling it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-10/
- The word for "kindness" is *hesed*, loyal love shown in action. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-10-commentary
- What kindness Nahash had shown? Keil and Delitzsch: we are not told in what the love shown to David by Nahash consisted. He had most likely rendered him some assistance during the time of his flight from Saul. Barnes adds that Nahash's hatred of Saul may have disposed him favorably toward Saul's enemy David. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/10-2.htm
- Gill (Baptist) reports a Jewish tradition. After the king of Moab killed David's family, one brother escaped, and Nahash protected him (Trapp gives the same story). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/10-2.html ; https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/2-samuel/10-2.html
- Is this the same Nahash who attacked Jabesh-gilead in 1 Samuel 11? Most say yes (Keil, JFB, Clarke). The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary disagrees: that siege was probably forty years after the event there recorded, it is more likely a son of the same name. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-samuel-10.html
- **Where readers differ: should David have reached out at all?**
  - Matthew Henry (Presbyterian): David doesn't pick apart why someone was kind to him; he simply repays it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_010.cfm
  - Henry also reports a harsher view. Some have thought that David, in the indignity he received from the king of Ammon, was but well enough served for courting and complimenting that pagan prince, given Deut. 23:3. (same URL)
  - Trapp rejects that view. He says the bad outcome doesn't prove David was wrong, as the scholar Pellican claimed, because duty is to be done, however it speed or take with wicked persons. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/2-samuel/10-2.html
- **Dating:** Constable says this must have taken place early in David's reign, probably after his goodness to Mephibosheth. (same URL)

**v. 3**
- Guzik: the princes may really have been suspicious, or may have wanted to look shrewd. It is common for liars to suspect others of lying. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-10/
- Henry: Unfounded suspicion argues a wicked mind. He sets this against "charity thinketh no evil." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_010.cfm
- Precept Austin: it's ironic that the king's counsellors doubted the other king's comforters. The lesson is to be careful whose advice you take. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-10-commentary
- Whedon: "the city" means Rabbah, Ammon's capital. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/2-samuel-10.html

**v. 4**
- Why this was so shameful:
  - Keil and Delitzsch: the beard was a man's greatest ornament, so cutting off half was the greatest insult that could have been offered to the ambassadors, and through them to David their king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/10-4.htm
  - Pulpit Commentary: the beard marked a free man, so this treated the envoys like slaves. Hanun intended this as a challenge to war, whereas David had meant peace and friendship. https://biblehub.com/2_samuel/10-4.htm
  - Clarke: The beard was never cut off but in *mourning*, or as a sign of *slavery*. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/10-4.html
- The cut garments: as the ancient Israelites wore no trousers, the lower half of the body was quite exposed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/10-4.htm
  - Trapp, quoted by Guzik, says the aim was also to expose their circumcision to mockery. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-10/
- Poole: the half-shave mocked the envoys by forcing on them a pagan mourning custom that Israelites were forbidden (Lev. 19:27). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/10-4.htm
- Gill (Baptist): the Ammonites probably sneered that since the men came to mourn, they should look like mourners. (same URL)
- Ellicott: It is remarkable that in none of David's wars does he appear as the aggressor. (same URL)
- **Lessons and Christ-centred readings:**
  - Henry: don't take unjust insults too much to heart. A damaged reputation in a little time grows again, as these beards did. (same URL)
  - BibleHub study notes see a picture of Christ. The envoys' disgrace foreshadowing the shame endured by Christ when He was rejected and mocked by those He came to bless. https://biblehub.com/2_samuel/10-4.htm
- **A different explanation of Hanun's motive:** Peake's Commentary, quoted by Coffman, suggests Hanun kept half the beards and garments as some guarantee of peace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/10-4.html

**v. 5**
- Guzik: David didn't use these men as political tools to whip up anger against the Ammonites. He cared more for their own dignity and honor. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-10/
- Henry: Jericho was a quiet place where they could stay out of sight until the shaved half grew long enough to trim the other half to match. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/10-4.html
- Whedon: being seen in that state would have exposed them to lasting ridicule. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/2-samuel-10.html

**v. 6**
- Guzik: David didn't reject the Ammonites; they **made themselves repulsive** to Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-10/
- Henry: Had they humbled themselves, and begged David's pardon, probably an honorary satisfaction might have atoned for the offence. He applies it to sinners who provoke God without counting the cost. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_010.cfm
- Whedon on the place names:
  - "King Maacah" should read "the king of Maacah"; Maacah is a place.
  - "Ish-tob" should read "men of Tob," the region where Jephthah fled.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/2-samuel-10.html
- **Order of events (debated):** Whedon thinks the Syrian conquests of chapter 8 actually came after this war; the order of chapters isn't the order of events. (same URL) Poole instead says the mention of Ammonite spoils in 8:12 is by way of anticipation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/10-2.htm

**v. 7**
- Guzik: this is the first time David's "mighty men" are mentioned. David was nothing without his mighty men, and they were nothing without him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-10/
- Henry: a good king keeps war as far from his own people as he can. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_010.cfm

**v. 8**
- Whedon:
  - The gate is the gate of Rabbah.
  - 1 Chronicles 19:7 places the Syrians at Medeba, some way south.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/2-samuel-10.html
- Constable also places the first battle at Medeba. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/10-12.html

**vv. 9–10**
- Guzik: Israel was boxed in, with Ammonites in front and Syrians behind. It looked bad for the army of Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-10/
- Whedon: Joab seems to have walked unknowingly into a position between Rabbah and Medeba. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/2-samuel-10.html
- Coffman: Joab saw the Syrian hired troops as the bigger threat, so he led his best men against them himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/10-12.html

**v. 11**
- Henry: Joab planned with his brother so that splitting the army wouldn't weaken it. Mutual helpfulness is brotherly duty. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_010.cfm
- G. Campbell Morgan, quoted by Guzik: Joab never seems to have considered that the combined enemy might beat them both. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-10/
- Whedon: the plan was for each brother to watch the other and help him, not to attack both armies at once. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/2-samuel-10.html

**v. 12**
- **"The cities of our God":**
  - Keil and Delitzsch: they fought in order that Jehovah's possessions might not fall into the hands of the heathen, and become subject to their gods. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/10-12.htm
  - Barnes: perhaps relieving the Israelite town of Medeba was in view, and keeping Molech worship from replacing the worship of the LORD. (same URL)
  - Whedon (Methodist): Israel was taught that its land belonged to God (Lev. 25:23). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/2-samuel-10.html
- **When war is right:** the Geneva Study Bible (Reformed) says this verse shows war should be fought for the defence of true religion and God's people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/10-12.htm
- **"May the LORD do…": a wish or a statement?**
  - The Hebrew literally reads "will do." Most translations make it a prayer; NET and NIV make it a statement. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-10-commentary
  - Ellicott: Rather, The Lord will do. He reads it as full trust in God's wisdom. https://biblehub.com/2_samuel/10-12.htm
  - Pulpit Commentary: They are the words not so much of confidence as of determined resolution. (same URL)
  - Henry: let God's work be done by us, and then God's will be done concerning us. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_010.cfm
- **Was Joab a man of faith? (differing views):**
  - Constable notes Joab's commendable spirituality in 2 Samuel 10:12. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/10-12.html
  - Kelly (Brethren) calls Joab a man as far as possible from the faith of David. He says letting Joab have such influence was one of the fatal weaknesses of David's kingdom. (same URL)
- **Sermon use:** older preachers apply it to Christians "playing the men" for the Church and for Christ their King. https://biblehub.com/sermons/2_samuel/10-12.htm

**v. 13**
- Guzik: the text doesn't even say a battle took place. The hired army ran because God was with them. God promised this kind of blessing upon an obedient Israel (Deuteronomy 28:7). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-10/
- Coffman: hired soldiers had no reason to die for Rabbah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/10-12.html

**v. 14**
- Whedon: the Ammonites shut themselves inside Rabbah. Joab thought a siege unwise at that point, which is picked up again in 11:1. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/2-samuel-10.html
- Guzik: Joab's army was kept safe, but they did not win a decisive victory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/

**vv. 15–16**
- Guzik: The enemies of Israel wouldn't quit after one defeat. They were a persistent enemy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-10/
- Whedon:
  - "Beyond the River" means beyond the Euphrates.
  - Helam lies east of the Jordan, but no one has found where.
  - Shobach was to Hadadezer what Joab was to David.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/2-samuel-10.html

**v. 17**
- Constable: Joab led first, but later David himself went into battle and led his soldiers (2 Samuel 10:17). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/10-12.html
- Guzik: David being there was a gracious warning from God that his leadership mattered. He ignored it, stayed in Jerusalem, and fell with Bathsheba. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-10/
- Guzik also notes elsewhere that this wasn't where David's slide began. David showed his disregard of God's plan for marriage many years before when he took more than one wife. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-11/

**v. 18: the numbers (700 vs. 7,000; horsemen vs. foot soldiers)**
The BSB reads "foot soldiers" here; the Hebrew has "horsemen" (Precept Austin's technical note). 1 Chronicles 19:18 has 7,000 charioteers and foot soldiers.
- **Two counts of the same thing (harmonising):**
  - Gill: 700 chariots at ten men each makes 7,000 men. He also suggests the same troops could ride to battle and fight on foot. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/10-18.htm
  - The Geneva notes and Poole: the 700 were the elite part of 7,000. (same URL)
- **Copying error, with Samuel's "700" correct:**
  - Barnes thinks 700 more likely, because numbers written as letters were easily confused. (same URL)
  - Whedon (Methodist) agrees it is doubtless the error of a copyist. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/2-samuel-10.html
- **Copying error, with Chronicles' "7,000" correct:** Walter Kaiser says 7,000 is right. He notes some Septuagintal texts of 2 Samuel 10:18 agree with Chronicles. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-10-commentary
- **Can't be resolved:**
  - Pulpit Commentary: It is impossible to reconcile these conflicting numbers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/10-18.htm
  - The Cambridge Bible suspects further copying errors. (same URL)
- **Modern scholarship (reported second-hand):** Utley sets two views side by side. The Jewish Study Bible says the Chronicler expands the numbers in 2 Samuel 10 to glorify David's victory. The NASB Study Bible (p. 577) says it was a copyist's mistake in Samuel. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-10-commentary
- **Theological reading:** BibleHub study notes treat the figures as literal historical totals; Scripture gives no hint they are symbolic. https://biblehub.com/2_samuel/10-18.htm

**v. 19**
- Whedon:
  - Hadadezer's officers seem to have made the peace for him; he wasn't there himself.
  - He links a later breach of this peace to the conquest of all Syria in chapter 8.
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/2-samuel-10.html
- JFB: after this decisive victory the small Syrian kingdoms submitted and paid tribute. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/10-18.htm
- Henry sums up the chapter. Thus did David advance his own reputation for gratitude, in returning kindness, and for justice, in repaying injuries. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_010.cfm
